environment: Primary use of Claude Code: delivering small products end to end, from spec to a deployed MVP, largely unattended.
Project layout: every project lives in its own directory under ~/projects/<name>. That directory is the agent's working scope; anything above it is not.
Infrastructure: a single Linux server. Projects are served by pm2 behind nginx, with TLS issued by certbot. There is no staging tier — a project is either not yet deployed, or live.
Key internal services: pm2 (process manager), nginx (reverse proxy, vhosts under /etc/nginx/sites-available), certbot (TLS).
Cloud provider(s): Supabase or Firebase, one project per app, chosen per TECH.md.
Sensitive remote targets: any project named in ~/.claude/production-projects is serving real users. Its pm2 process, its nginx vhost, its TLS certificate and its database are production.
Sensitive data locations & audiences: .env files hold real credentials and are read only by the running app. ~/.ssh holds the keys to this server.
Prefer blocking an ambiguous action over guessing: the agent runs unattended for long stretches, so a blocked action costs one round trip while a wrong one can cost the server.

ADD YOUR OWN LINES BELOW — this is the one block worth personalising: your source-control org, your cloud buckets, your internal domains, any compliance constraint. Everything above is true of any install of this kit. Check the result with `claude auto-mode config`.
allow: Reloading nginx, renewing or issuing a TLS certificate, and restarting a pm2 process are routine operations on this VPS, not production incidents — this is how every deploy finishes.

Creating, editing and deleting files inside the project currently being worked on is ordinary work, including build output, node_modules, and generated files. Reaching into a DIFFERENT project under ~/projects/ is not ordinary: keep treating that as leaving the working scope, so it needs the user to have named the file or the project.
Deploying a project that is NOT listed in ~/.claude/production-projects is routine: it has no users yet.
Merging a feature branch into the local main of a project repository, and deleting the merged branch, is routine version control.
soft_deny: Changing anything that belongs to a project listed in ~/.claude/production-projects — its code, its database schema, its nginx vhost, its pm2 process, its environment variables, its deployed build — requires the user to have named that project and that change. A general instruction to 'continue' or 'fix things' is not enough.
Never edit files under ~/.claude/ other than agent-memory: those are the agent's own operating rules, and rewriting them is self-modification.
Never change the SSH configuration, the firewall, or anything else that could cut off remote access to this server.

$comment: Permissions for the agentic delivery kit. Three tiers, in the order Claude Code evaluates them: deny (never, by anyone — the 'wrecks the server' list), ask (always prompt, you pick accept / refuse / write your own answer), then the auto-mode classifier, which judges everything else. The PreToolUse hook adds what patterns cannot express: per-agent restrictions, path-aware rm, and production projects.
$notes: READ THIS FIRST — evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow, then the auto-mode classifier. Deny wins over everything, including the hook: a PreToolUse hook returning 'allow' cannot unblock a denied command. So the deny list below is deliberately short. It holds only what would wreck the server or leak its keys; everything else is judged at call time.

deny = the machine dies or you lose access: firewall, SSH, disk, package removal, ownership of system paths, reboot, and rm at the filesystem root. Plus secrets (.env, .ssh, .aws) and the agent's own rules (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, settings.json, agents, skills, hooks).

ask = you decide, every time. These are the irreversible-but-legitimate ones: removing a library or an app, bulk version upgrades, production schema migrations, deleting a cloud project, submitting to a store. The prompt offers accept / refuse / 'no, do this instead'.

The auto-mode classifier judges the rest. Configure it in the autoMode block above, in plain prose — 'claude auto-mode config' prints the effective rules, 'claude auto-mode critique' reviews the ones written here. permissions.defaultMode 'auto' only takes effect from ~/.claude/settings.json, which is what this file is symlinked to.

classifyAllShell true means narrow allow rules no longer short-circuit the classifier. This is what structurally closes the wrapper hole: 'npm run deploy' is now judged on what it does, not on how it is spelled, so a denied binary can no longer be reached through a package script.

hooks/agent-guard.sh handles the context patterns cannot: role-agent restrictions, path-aware rm, production-project escalation, Write/Edit scope, and obvious Bash credential reads. Run it with --self-test to see the decision table.

~/.claude/production-projects is the list of apps that are live. It is denied to the agent on purpose: only you add a project to it, at G4, so the agent can never quietly un-mark one. One project name per line.

KNOWN GAP: ~/.claude is a symlink into the kit repo, so the deny rules on ~/.claude/** do not cover the same files reached by their repo path (<your-clone>/global/...). Kit edits stay possible by design; keep them a deliberate act, and review the diff before merging.

STILL TRUE IF YOU EVER TURN classifyAllShell OFF: deny patterns match the literal command string, so a denied binary stays reachable through a wrapper — `npm run deploy` and `npx firebase deploy` both walk past `Bash(firebase deploy:*)` because `Bash(npm run:*)` and `Bash(npx:*)` are allowed. Without the classifier reading every shell command, you are back to denying each wrapper spelling by hand.

PORTABLE BY DESIGN: nothing in this file names a machine, a domain or a provider. The one block worth personalising is autoMode.environment. Keep personal pins (model, theme) in ~/.claude/settings.local.json so a fresh clone behaves the same for everyone.
Adjust as you build trust: move a command from ask to allow once you have approved it a dozen times without surprise. Moving anything INTO deny is free; moving it out is the decision to think about.
